title: Testing honey moisture before bottling
subtitle: The one check that decides whether your honey stores or ferments.
excerpt: Honey with more than 20% water will ferment in the jar, souring a whole harvest in weeks. A refractometer check takes one small sample from each bucket and gives a reading in under a minute. Here is how to calibrate, sample, and read the result.
sourceNotes: NBU Beekeeper's Toolkit (2024), section on honey quality and harvest. British Honey Importers and Packers Association, Honey Quality Standards. Frank Pearson, Bee-keeping for All (1923), Internet Archive, notes on syrup density and harvest timing.

glossaryTerms.definition: A scale for measuring dissolved sugar concentration in a liquid. For honey, 79–80 Brix corresponds to roughly 17–18% water content.
The breakdown of sugars by wild yeasts into alcohol and carbon dioxide. In honey, fermentation is triggered when water content exceeds 20% and wild yeast populations are present.

content.text: Honey that has not been capped by the bees, or has been extracted too early, may carry more than 20% water. That is the threshold above which wild yeasts activate and
fermentation
begins. Test every extraction bucket before you bottle, not after.
Calibrating the refractometer

Calibrate before the first reading of each session. Place one drop of distilled water on the prism, close the daylight plate, and hold the refractometer toward a light source. The reading should fall at 0% water content on the honey scale, which corresponds to 100 on the
Brix
scale. If it does not, turn the calibration screw until the line sits on 0. Wipe the prism dry with a soft cloth before taking a honey reading.
Taking the sample
Stir the honey bucket gently before sampling. Moisture can stratify, with wetter honey rising to the surface if the extraction included uncapped or lightly capped frames.
Dip a clean knife or spatula and take a small smear, about the size of a pea. Place it on the prism.
Close the daylight plate carefully to spread the honey into a thin, even film. Avoid trapping air bubbles.
Look through the eyepiece. A clear horizontal line divides a blue upper field from a bright lower field. Read the water-content number where the line crosses the percentage scale.
Wipe the prism clean with a damp soft cloth between buckets.
Reading the result
Below 17%: excellent. Long shelf life. Most heather and clover honey from well-capped frames reads here.
17–20%: safe to bottle. Will keep well for at least two years.
20–23%: borderline. Some batches at 20–21% stabilise; others ferment within months. See the handling section below.
Above 23%: do not bottle as table honey. The batch needs immediate attention.
Handling honey that reads above 20%

Honey above 20% water should not be blended with dry honey and bottled. Options are: blend it into mead, where fermentation is intended; use it as winter feed syrup for the bees; or pass it through a warming cabinet at 35°C for 24 hours to evaporate some moisture. The warming cabinet method works only if the reading is borderline (21 to 22%) and the honey is stirred periodically to allow surface evaporation.

attrs.cue: Blurry or double line on the prism — cannot read the scale
attrs.cause: Air bubble trapped under the daylight plate, or the honey film is uneven
attrs.fix: Lift the plate, wipe clean, and re-apply the sample. Make sure the honey covers the whole prism surface before closing the plate.

attrs.cue: The scale appears at the wrong angle or the line is curved
attrs.cause: The daylight plate is dirty or fogged from a previous sample
attrs.fix: Clean the plate with a damp cloth. Very cold honey can also cause this; let the honey reach room temperature before testing.

attrs.cue: Reading is consistent at 0% for every sample
attrs.cause: The calibration step was not carried out, or distilled water is still on the prism
attrs.fix: Wipe the prism thoroughly after calibration, then re-test the honey.
